svg.text: K1 — Ceiling turret cell: how the mechanisms work
Six close-ups, each looping. Orange = moving mechanism, steel blue = loose stainless ware, yellow = food, blue = water.

g.text: Turret: two discs place the rod
Two rotations of the ceiling discs move the rod to any point
inside a Ø400 circle; the rod slides up and down (Z) and
turns (yaw). All motors sit above the ceiling, in the dry.
4 tool lifts out of the rail
No gripper, no tool changer: a bayonet on the rod tip.
Carries 300 N push, 100 N pull, 20 Nm; 6–8 s per change.
Tools hang on rails that leave the cell with them.
move 1: T1 swings the cup onto the turntable
move 2: turntable half turn hands it to T2
move 3: T2 swings it to the bench edge
move 4: T3 takes it over the hob
tool reach Ø780 with the roll head
Rod reach Ø400 per turret (42 % of the deck); circles never meet.
The roll head adds 190 mm, so hands hand over: ≈ 5 moves
and 50 s per vessel to the hobs; 110–280 moves per meal.
In operation: filtered air blows down the gap
In the wash: jets flush the gap, water drips out
Ceiling seam: an open gap, not a seal
Food sees only a smooth 4 mm gap behind a 45 mm coaming; the
only seal sits on the dry side. Untested: can the fixed wall be
Dicing under the fixed press ram
The ram pushes the piece through the grid in 10 mm steps; a hand
sweeps the cut-off blade. Press load goes into the wall pegs,
not the turrets. 0.9–2.3 kN; 1.5 kg potatoes in 3 min.
1 pan B, preheated, is set upside down on pan A
2 slid 8 mm: hook tabs lock, half stubs form one stub
3 roll head lifts the pair 160 mm, rolls 180°
4 set down; empty pan A is lifted off
Flipping a pancake: pan pair in the air
Two pans locked rim to rim are turned over by one roll head
Untested: fat at the rim, warped pans (risk 3).
